# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding
When choosing where to hide, favor central positions (4-6) in early rounds to maintain flexibility. As the game progresses and you accumulate targeting data on opponents, shift away from recently hit locations and away from positions you've used recently. Never return to a cell where you were hit in the immediately preceding round. In mid-to-late game, when no hits have landed across multiple rounds, interpret this as a sign that central positions are being actively avoided by all players—shift toward off-center but not extreme positions (2-3, 7-8) to exploit this avoidance pattern. However, recognize that other players may be making the same inference about off-center positions, so expect clustering there as well. Adjust accordingly based on emerging patterns.

## Station Notes
Post brief, cooperative notes early to establish credibility and encourage information sharing. Mirror the tone of the picket once a pattern emerges—if others signal stability, match that signal. Use notes to appear reliable without revealing strategic information. Maintain consistency with established signals through the final round, as this reinforces credibility. Understand that consistent "steady on station" notes from multiple players may indicate a cooperative consensus on avoiding high-risk behavior.

## Firing
Always follow standing orders unless you have strong tactical reasons to deviate. When firing under standing order, choose your cell strategically based on opponent patterns you've observed. In early rounds with no data, central positions (4-6) are reasonable. However, recognize that after multiple rounds with zero hits fleet-wide, opponents are likely avoiding central clustering—adjust fire locations accordingly rather than continuing to shoot the same central cells. Avoid concentrating all fire on positions you've previously fired at without results. After 5+ rounds with consistent misses against the same target, assume that target has learned your firing patterns and is actively avoiding your preferred cells—vary your fire more widely or consider whether the standing order target is actually following an exploitable pattern. Don't assume central positions work just because they worked in early game.

## Making Claims
Always claim truthfully what the office told you. The credibility cost of being caught in a false claim outweighs any single-round advantage, especially when playing multiple rounds. This applies even in final rounds. Truthful claiming preserves reputation for potential future encounters. Understand that building credibility through honest claims is a long-term strategy; a single loss (-1 point) from honest play is acceptable if it means your claims remain trusted.

## Escort Claims
Track which boats appear to be working together through their notes and behavior. When you escort, name a boat that has signaled stability or cooperation. Don't claim escorts you haven't actually secured—wait for clear evidence of mutual positioning. If uncertain, claim none rather than guess. Truthful escort claims maintain credibility. Recognize that mutual escort claims are rare and require explicit coordination signals beyond just consistent notes.

## General Strategy
Early game: Build credibility through honest play and cooperative signals. Gather baseline data on opponent behavior.
Mid game: Begin collecting targeting data on each opponent; note their hiding patterns. When a pattern of zero hits emerges across the fleet, interpret this as convergence toward avoidance of central positions rather than random distribution. Expect other players to make the same inference, which means off-center positions will also become congested.
Late game: Execute fire based on accumulated evidence, but maintain honesty in all claims to preserve reputation. In final rounds, recognize that if you've been missing the same target for 5+ rounds, your firing strategy against them is predictable and ineffective—they are successfully evading. A final round miss after many misses suggests the game may end in mutual stalemate rather than dramatic hits. Accept this outcome rather than abandon credibility for a desperate guess.

Never fire on Harbor unless the payoff is worth the threat—their ability to jettison makes that a costly engagement.

Recognize that sometimes the best outcome of a game is to end with your credibility intact and a modest loss, rather than to chase points through risky or deceptive plays that could backfire.

# Foxtrot Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding Strategy
When choosing a hiding cell, avoid the center positions (4-6) as they're predictable and easy to target. After being hit, immediately shift away from recently used cells. Vary my position across the full range 1-9 rather than clustering in a comfort zone. Track which cells I've used and which cells have been targeted at me, then hide in cells I haven't occupied recently. Corner and edge positions (1-3, 7-9) are safer than central territory when under sustained fire. Position 2 worked well early—remember that edge positions without being too extreme can serve as reliable anchors when I need to break an attacker's pattern.

## Firing
When my standing order is to fire at a target, execute it reliably. Don't deviate from the standing order without strong tactical reason. Fire at cells that vary my attack pattern rather than repeating the same coordinate. If I hit, I've identified a viable cell; don't assume the target will return to it immediately. Accept that in a game with many miss streaks, maintaining consistent execution matters more than constantly chasing new strategies. Even hitting once per six rounds (as I did against Gamma in round 5) contributes to my point total. Stick with the standing order firing discipline.

## Claims
Always claim the true result that the office reports. Lying about claims creates no scoring advantage and risks credibility damage. Maintain honest claims to keep my word reliable. This episode confirmed that truthful claiming works—I claimed correctly every time and maintained credibility throughout.

## Escort Claims
Actively use escort claims to generate points. This episode I still defaulted to "none" on most rounds and left significant points on the table. Initiate escort claims from round 1 with boats I'm not firing at (Echo or Gamma depending on round), and reciprocate immediately when another boat names me. Don't wait for perfect information—act on the game structure. Two mutual escorts generate 10 points per round for both parties—this is the primary scoring channel and shouldn't be left on the table. In my last-round escort claim to Echo, I finally acted on this logic and it was the right move. Make this my default strategy from round 1 onward, not a last-resort tactic.

## Harbor Consideration
Never fire on Harbor. The payoff structure is designed against it. Harbor's threat is real and the standing order doesn't require firing on them. Accept the constraint.

## General Approach
I ended this episode with 12 points, a significant improvement over my 0-point previous game. The improvement came from:
- One successful hit against Gamma in round 5 (4 points + escort payoff = 7 points of the total)
- Finally initiating a mutual escort claim with Echo in round 6 (5 points)
- Maintaining reliable execution of my standing order throughout

But I still left points on the table. I should have:
- Initiated mutual escort claims with Echo starting in round 2 (when I'm not my firing at them), creating a 5-round partnership worth 25 points
- Been more aggressive about reading the patrol log and matching escort patterns earlier

Next episode: Start escort coordination in round 1 or 2. Name Echo as escort in rounds 2-4 when I'm firing at Gamma, then name Gamma as escort in rounds 5-6. Don't default to "none"—treat escort claims as my primary scoring mechanism. Maintain my hiding discipline and honest firing claims. The combination of reliable execution plus active escort coordination should yield 30+ points.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding
When choosing where to hide, I will track which cells my shooters have targeted in recent rounds and rotate away from those specific cells. I will vary my choice unpredictably rather than favoring edges or centers consistently. However, I should recognize that with limited rounds and a small board, pattern-breaking may have diminishing returns—I cannot avoid all previously-shot cells indefinitely. I will prioritize avoiding the most recent fire cell rather than building complex multi-round rotation schemes. When I take a hit, I will rotate to a different region of the board (e.g., if hit in the center, move to an edge) rather than returning to the same area.

## Firing
When I am assigned to fire under standing order, I will track my target's actual hiding positions across multiple rounds and identify their true hiding pattern, not just their last position. If I have hit a target before (as I did with Echo in round 1), I should test whether they return to that cell or rotate away. After multiple consecutive misses at the same cell (five misses at Echo's position 5), I should acknowledge that the target has learned to avoid it and shift my fire cell accordingly rather than repeating the same failed shot. I will vary my fire cell from round to round based on observed movement, not just repeat what worked once.

## Claiming
When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I will always claim that result truthfully. False claims cost credibility, and in a game where patterns and trust matter, integrity on mandatory claims is more valuable than a single-round advantage. I have verified this principle works—my final score of +1, though modest, reflects honest play without credibility damage.

## Station Notes
When posting station notes, I will use consistent language like "steady on station" as a default unless I have a specific reason to signal something. Consistency itself is the signal, and changing notes only creates noise without clear benefit.

## Escort Claims
When choosing an escort claim, I need to actively build mutual escort relationships early in the game rather than defaulting to "none." I will name a specific boat as my escort claim starting from round 2 and watch whether they reciprocate. If they do, I will continue reciprocating in subsequent rounds to secure the 5-point bonus. I will not abandon the escort strategy passively—each round I must either commit to testing a boat or consciously accept the cost of claiming none. If a boat does not reciprocate after I name them, I can switch targets or claim "none," but I should not treat "none" as a safe default. The escort system is a significant source of points and requires early active commitment to be effective. I should track escort reciprocations throughout the game and identify which boats are willing to mutual-claim with me.

## General Strategy
I will track the standing order rotation to know which boat is shooting at whom each round. I will monitor scores and recognize which boats are winning. I will accept that defensive hiding is more reliable than offensive predictive firing when patterns are unclear, but I should not fire the same cell repeatedly after multiple misses—this is ineffective and wastes rounds. I will use the escort claim system actively from round 2 onward rather than treating it as optional. Most importantly: my first episode score was +1, which is minimal. The escort system appears to be where significant points accumulate, and I failed to engage with it meaningfully by repeatedly claiming "none." Next episode, I will commit to naming a specific boat for escort starting in round 2 and maintain that relationship if they reciprocate.
